topic: Rutis: a five-pillar agent kernel in idiomatic Rust (Cordis paradigm port)
summary: rutis is a single-maintainer Rust workspace that reimplements the Cordis plugin paradigm (the TypeScript framework vendored inside DeepSeek Harness) as a five-pillar kernel - plugin as unit of assembly, fiber as lifecycle container, typed-key service registry, four-dispatch-semantics event bus, dependency-driven reload - and then layers a deliberately minimal coding-agent framework on top of it via the aimux LanguageModel seam. The honest read for a 'rust agent framework' buyer: the kernel is the product and the agent is a sample. rutis-agent ships one tool registry plugin, one driver plugin, an in-memory session and a ratatui TUI with two built-in tools (bash, replace_text); it is not a competitor to Rig or AutoAgents on agent features, and its own README calls it 'a minimal coding agent sample'. What is genuinely unusual is the engineering evidence: 96 upstream Cordis specs audited line by line with 58 language-agnostic invariants locked by automated parity tests, 141 kernel contract/differential tests, a published event-dispatch benchmark that refuses to claim victory on nanosecond deltas, and design docs that name what is NOT done. The two blocking facts for adoption are supply chain and API churn: the workspace moved from eric8810/rutis to the arcships org during September 2026 (crate versions 0.1.0 -> 0.2.x -> 0.3.0 -> 0.5.0 in six weeks), the crate published from the old repo already requires sibling-only path dependencies, and rutis-cordis / rutis-dsh / aimux-llm are not on crates.io at all, so consumers must build from git.

key_facts.what_it_is: A five-pillar plugin/lifecycle kernel ('Rust plugin framework' in the current README) plus a minimal agent framework layered on the aimux unified-LLM service. Not a batteries-included agent product.

five_pillars: Plugin = unit of assembly: one apply() provides services / registers listeners / registers cleanup, exactly once

Fiber = lifecycle container: six-state machine (Pending, Loading, Active, Failed, Unloading, Disposed) + dependency gating + cascading unload + exactly-once LIFO cleanup with atomic rollback of half-registered resources
Service = typed registry: TypeKey identifies the service by type instead of a string key; isolate scopes; qualified keys allow multiple instances of one interface
Event bus = four dispatch semantics: emit (ordered per key) / parallel (concurrent fan-out) / serial (first-value short-circuit) / waterfall (middleware chain with next())
Dependency-driven reload: when a provider unloads, its consumers are evicted and reloaded automatically without being touched by application code
key_facts.agent_framework: Six elements: LLM backend (Arc<dyn LanguageModel> service from aimux, consumed not re-declared), ToolRegistry (plugin), session (in-memory ordered messages, deliberately NOT a plugin - it is the single source of truth for the loop and lives in the driver's fiber), agent loop (a driver plugin implementing the Agent interface), event observation (agent/* broadcasts plus waterfalls at agent/pre-step, agent/request, tools/pre-execute, execute, post-execute), minimal mode tools (bash + replace_text). TUI via rutui (ratatui 0.29 / crossterm 0.28) with streaming, tool visibility and Esc cancel.
key_facts.parity_with_cordis: All 96 upstream Cordis spec cases read line by line; 58 language-agnostic invariants locked by automated parity tests (31 full + 27 partial per the parity ruling table); 38 not ported with a declared reason each (JS-specific mechanisms: Proxy, string event names, internal/*, sync bail, traceable/caller-shadow, Context.filter, intercept, async generator effect, update config). Deliberate strengthenings: cross-effect cleanup is strictly serial LIFO (upstream Cordis runs them concurrently) and per-key emit ordering was rebuilt explicitly.
key_facts.verification_layers: Unit (ScriptedLlm implements the real LanguageModel including do_stream - loop logic, multi-turn history, max_steps, cancellation, failure feedback) / integration (aimux MockReplayModel record+replay - dual gating, unload-llm-triggers-evict-and-reload, fiber unload cancels in-flight work, event observation) / real end-to-end (#[ignore], requires DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, does not run in CI)
key_facts.third_party_coverage: Hysen Labs published an independent analysis (editorial dated 2026-08-26, data snapshot 2026-09-27); it is the only non-author coverage found, and it already describes superseded facts (it says the kernel README claims 115 contract tests and that the last push was 2026-08-19).
key_facts.independent_signal: Featured on Trendshift (repository 167702); the author's announcement post on X (@ashfold) frames it as a Rust rewrite of Cordis with a minimal-mode agent example that runs after exporting a DeepSeek key, and jokes about trying self-evolution next. competitors.name: cordis (upstream, TypeScript) - the paradigm rutis ports
key_points: 8,896 stars, 554 forks, MIT, created 2022-05-17, last push 2026-09-08 - roughly 400x rutis's star count.
Now documented as the plugin framework vendored inside DeepSeek Harness (deepseek-harness.github.io/reference/cordis-primer), which makes this paradigm production-relevant rather than academic.
Cordis's own five concepts: plugin, context (services live at stable ctx.<key>), inject dependency declaration, typed events, reversible registrations via ctx.effect()/ctx.on().
Cordis documents five dispatch modes (emit, waterfall, parallel, serial, bail); rutis exposes four (emit/parallel/serial/waterfall) and folds the bail case into serial's first-value short-circuit.
The primer states Cordis dispatch mode is part of an event's public contract and is checked against the event catalogue - the same discipline rutis inherits.
competitors.why_competes: Any decision to use rutis is really a decision to use Cordis semantics in Rust. Cordis is the mature, populated, feature-complete option; rutis is the port with type safety and a single binary but a fraction of the surface.

competitors.name: Rig - the default Rust agent/LLM library
key_points: 8,766 stars, 981 forks, created 2024-06-05, last push 2026-09-29 - actively maintained and by far the most adopted Rust LLM/agent stack.
Crate-level scale: rig-core has 3,115,669 total downloads, 1,684,403 in the recent window, current version 0.42.0 - versus rutis's 197 lifetime downloads.

Positioning per rig.rs: one composable trait system from single completion to tools, streaming, RAG and multi-agent workflows; 20+ providers behind one API; typed tools and structured output; mock models and VCR cassette tests for determinism.

Benchmark position (third-party, Jan 2026): 6,065 ms average latency, 4.44 rps, 1,019 MB peak memory, 24.3% CPU, ~4 ms cold start - the most CPU-efficient framework measured, but no plugin lifecycle or hot reload.
Licence is reported inconsistently across sources (GitHub API says MIT; a competitor's comparison table lists Apache-2.0) - verify before relying on it.
competitors.why_competes: If the job is 'build an LLM app or agent in Rust', Rig is the incumbent answer and needs no kernel. rutis only wins if the requirement is loadable/unloadable capability plugins with dependency-driven reload - a different requirement, not a better Rig.

competitors.name: AutoAgents - multi-agent framework with actor model and WASM tool sandbox
key_points: 761 stars, 88 forks, Apache-2.0, created 2025-02-22, last push 2026-08-26; crate 'autoagents' has 15,196 total downloads (4,364 recent), current 0.4.0.

Architecture: Ractor (Erlang/OTP-style actor model) for agent coordination, typed pub/sub for multi-agent orchestration, Basic and ReAct executors, derive macros for tools and structured outputs, sliding-window memory with pluggable backends, sandboxed WASM tool execution, OpenTelemetry tracing.
Benchmark position (same third-party suite): highest composite score at 5,714 ms average latency, 9,652 ms P95, 4.97 rps, 1,046 MB peak, 29.2% CPU, 4 ms cold start.
Its own claim in the same article: 25% better latency than average Python frameworks and 43.7% better than LangGraph; 36% more throughput than the Python average.
Ecosystem research (zylos.ai, 2026-04-01) argues the actor model gives supervision trees and location transparency, and that WASM sandboxing with fuel metering is the emerging tool-isolation answer.
competitors.why_competes: This is what a Rust agent framework looks like when the framework, not the kernel, is the product. rutis has no multi-agent orchestration, no sandbox, no executors and no guardrails - it has lifecycle.

competitors.name: Third-party benchmark: Rust vs Python agent frameworks (Jan 2026)
key_points: Method: 50 requests, 10 concurrent, gpt-5.1 across all frameworks, identical hardware, no CPU pinning; measures P50/P95/P99, throughput, peak RSS, CPU, cold start and determinism.
Headline structural result: Rust frameworks peak at ~1.0-1.1 GB while every Python framework measured exceeded 4.7 GB - a ~5x memory difference at 50 concurrent instances (~51 GB versus ~279 GB).
Cold start: AutoAgents and Rig ~4 ms versus 54-63 ms for LangChain, PydanticAI, LlamaIndex and LangGraph, and 138 ms for TS-based GraphBit.
Latency is dominated by the LLM network round trip, so all frameworks cluster between 5.7 s and 7.0 s; framework overhead only becomes visible at P95 (LangGraph 16,891 ms versus AutoAgents 9,652 ms).
Composite weighting is latency 27.8%, throughput 33.3%, memory 22.2%, CPU efficiency 16.7% - read scores with that weighting in mind.
Caveat for any 'rutis is fast' argument: this suite does not measure plugin lifecycle, reload or eviction cost, which is exactly rutis's claim to fame.
competitors.why_competes: Any review of a Rust agent framework has to position it against this data, and note that rutis appears in none of it - it publishes its own event-dispatch microbenchmark instead.

competitors.name: Hysen Labs - independent analysis of rutis (the only third-party coverage found)
key_points: Correctly identifies the target user: 'Rust developers building a host process that loads and unloads capability plugins at runtime, not someone who wants an agent binary', and calls the agent framework a demonstration that the kernel holds up.
Explicit don't-adopt-as-a-coding-agent verdict, citing the crates.io rutis-cli lag and the #[ignore] real-backend tests.
Flags the coupling trade-off honestly: 'your plugins have to declare dependencies in the kernel's terms, and the kernel owns their lifetime'.
Notes MIT permits commercial and closed-source use with attribution, licence inherited from Cordis (Shigma).
Already stale: it reports 115 kernel contract tests (current README says 141), a last push of 2026-08-19, and 21 stars - it predates the arcships move and the 0.3.0/0.5.0 releases.
competitors.why_competes: Not a competitor: it is the baseline of existing coverage a new review must beat, and its staleness is itself a data point about how fast the project moves.

competitors.name: aimux - the LLM seam rutis-agent consumes
key_points: 195 stars, created 2026-07-28, last push 2026-09-29; same org as the current rutis repo.
Positioning: unified LLM access layer for Rust - repo description says 325 providers; the rutis READMEs (both old and current) say 329. The discrepancy is unresolved in the sources.

rutis-agent and rutis-cli consume aimux-core / aimux-providers from crates.io (0.3.0), so no sibling checkout is needed - the README explicitly says a local aimux hack only requires an uncommitted [patch] at the workspace root.
This is the layer rutis delegates all provider concerns to, which is why rutis-agent is small: no HTTP clients, no auth, no streaming protocol of its own.
competitors.why_competes: It is the reason the agent crate is minimal, and it is the same org's asset - evaluating rutis-agent means evaluating aimux plus a driver loop plus a TUI, with aimux doing the heavy lifting.

angles: The keyword is 'rust agent framework' but the crate is a plugin framework. rutis's own README titles it 'A plugin framework for Rust' and files rutis-agent/rutis-cli under 'Built with rutis'. A review must say this plainly: you are evaluating a lifecycle kernel with an agent-shaped demo, not an agent framework. That reframing is the single most useful thing the article can do for a reader who arrived from the keyword.

Read the move, not the release notes: the same 243-commit history now lives at arcships/rutis, the crates.io repo field was repointed from eric8810 to arcships, and the version went 0.1.0 -> 0.5.0 between 2026-08-19 and 2026-09-28. Nine releases in six weeks with an unpublished 0.4.0 means the public API is moving under you; the repo also ships migration guides for both 0.1->0.2 and 0.3->0.5, which is unusual honesty for a project this young.

The 'just declare dependencies and the kernel owns the lifetime' trade is the whole product. Dependency-driven reload - unload the llm provider and its consumers are evicted and reloaded without application code - is a capability that neither Rig nor AutoAgents nor the Python frameworks in the benchmark suite offer. The cost is that every component must declare its dependencies in the kernel's terms and surrender its start/stop schedule to the kernel.

Cordis parity as an engineering-evidence story: 96 upstream specs read line by line, 58 invariants locked by automated differential tests, and 38 explicitly NOT ported with a reason per case (Proxy, string event names, sync bail, caller-shadow, async generator effects). Almost no young open-source project publishes its non-goals as a ruling table. This is the strongest thing in the whole repo and it is invisible from the star count.

The two deliberate divergences from upstream are the interesting design choices: cross-effect cleanup is strictly serial LIFO where Cordis runs effects concurrently (a determinism-for-throughput trade), and per-key emit ordering had to be rebuilt explicitly because JS object key ordering does not exist in Rust.

Performance evidence worth trusting precisely because it is modest: the event-dispatch benchmark reports +5.9% ns/op on the empty exact-dispatch path and states outright that nanosecond differences must not be treated as cross-machine conclusions, that CPU frequency was not pinned and there are no confidence intervals. Compare that with the marketing-grade '43% lower overhead' claims elsewhere in the agent-OS space.

The honest gap list: no multi-agent orchestration, no tool sandbox, no guardrails, no retry/rollback policy documented for a failed reload, real-provider tests excluded from CI behind #[ignore], and the agent ships exactly two tools (bash, replace_text). Anyone expecting a coding agent should be told to look at dimcode (same org, 37 stars) or the incumbent CLIs instead.

The interop roadmap is where the ambition actually is: a dylib SDK for first-party plugins (load new plugin code without republishing the host, shared Rust types, no serialization, version rejection before load) and a design proposal for protocol plugins that mount TS Cordis plugins and Rust rutis plugins into one object space through proxies. Both are explicitly not finished - the protocol work is a design document with no implementation.

The dual-core doctrine is a rare piece of written strategy: rutis is the Rust spine, dsh (TS) is the laboratory, 'TS is the lab, Rust graduates', with explicit rustification criteria (semantics converged, mechanism not wording, distribution-sensitive, not npm-bound, on a trust boundary) and an explicit promise that prompt ASSEMBLY mechanism rustifies while prompt CONTENT never does. That is a testable rule, not a slogan, and the article can hold them to it.

Naming and discovery are a real adoption tax here: the crate name collides with recurrent urinary tract infection in search results, there is an unrelated routis CLI on crates.io and a rudis mini-Redis, and there is no Hacker News thread for rutis at all. For a framework whose pitch is 'adopt this kernel', discoverability is below the threshold where the evidence gets read.

H2: The fiber state machine and exactly-once cleanup (why the kernel is the product)

notes_for_writer: Type is 'review', so the verdict stance is expected: adopt / trial / hold. Recommended stance for this one: 'trial for plugin hosts, hold for agent builders' - be explicit that the keyword and the product disagree.

Lead paragraph should answer directly: rutis is a Rust reimplementation of the Cordis five-pillar plugin kernel with a minimal agent example layered on top; it is an agent kernel, not an agent framework.
Do not describe rutis as production-ready at scale. Evidence supports: 21 stars, one contributor, 197 crate downloads, nine releases in six weeks, git-only companion crates.

Use the Cordis parity numbers (96 reviewed / 58 locked / 38 refused with reasons) as the credibility centerpiece - it is the most verifiable claim in the project and no other young framework publishes a non-goal ruling table.

Cite the dispatch benchmark with the authors' own caveat attached (no confidence intervals, no CPU frequency pinning, not cross-machine conclusions). Do not present nanoseconds as a competitive advantage over Rig/AutoAgents.
Be explicit that rutis is absent from the widely cited Rust-vs-Python agent benchmark suite; the 'Rust is 5x lighter' numbers belong to Rig and AutoAgents, not to rutis.
Do not repeat the third-party 115-test figure as current - the current README says 141; and the Hysen analysis still shows the 2026-08-19 push as latest, which is stale.
Provider counts differ between sources (329 in both rutis READMEs, 325 in the aimux repo description). State the range or note the discrepancy rather than picking one.

Include the crates.io trap concretely: rutis-agent 0.2.0 depends on rutis ^0.2.0 and sibling rutui crates, while the current main workspace is 0.5.0 and uses rutui 0.1.0 from crates.io - the published agent is older than the repository, so pin carefully or build from git.

If mentioning the 'agent OS' category, keep it short and factual: rutis makes no such claim; it is a plugin kernel with an agent sample, and the ambitious parts (dylib plugin SDK, cross-language protocol plugins) are unfinished design work.

FAQ should cover: is rutis free (MIT, yes), does it need an API key (no - --scripted and tui_scripted run offline), what Rust version (1.85), does it work with local models (yes, AIMUX_PROVIDER=ollama AIMUX_MODEL=qwen3:8b), and is it the same as Cordis (no - an idiomatic Rust implementation of the paradigm, not a translation).
